headline: High: shared file access and broad egress create data-leak and cascading-error risks; prompt injection is limited by no shared channel.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ChatGPT Desktop can read files and clipboard, while slim reads and writes filesystem artifacts, so a manual file bridge is plausible. However, neither profile shows a default shared channel like MCP or direct ingestion of the other’s outputs, so the injection path is limited and not automatic.
conditions: IF the operator copies agent_b output into a file that agent_a reads
IF agent_a is prompted to treat file contents as instructions
mitigations: Keep outputs in separate folders
Disable copy-paste between agents during review
Add a fixed instruction prefix that tells agent_a to ignore embedded commands
Review any file passed from agent_b before agent_a opens it

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can read files, and agent_b can write filesystem artifacts while handling registry credentials and private keys; agent_a also touches uploaded files, screenshots, voice, and connected IDE code. In a shared workspace, sensitive material can flow from one agent to the other, and agent_b’s broad egress increases exfiltration risk.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or mounted directory
IF agent_b processes files containing secrets or private keys
IF agent_a is given screenshots or uploaded files from the same project
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for each agent
Remove secrets from shared directories before running either agent
Restrict agent_b to non-sensitive inputs only
Rotate any credentials exposed to agent_b
Audit outputs for leaked file contents before sharing them onward

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent_b has shell, subprocess, and write access, while agent_a has read-only filesystem access and vendor-only egress. They do not both write the same state by default, so direct write-write conflict is limited, but overlapping access to shared files can still cause racey edits if the operator points them at the same directory.
conditions: IF both agents are assigned the same writable directory through the orchestrator
IF agent_b modifies files that agent_a is simultaneously reading
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories
Serialize edits through one agent at a time
Use file snapshots before handing work to agent_a
Avoid concurrent runs on the same repository

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent_a can produce screenshots, file-derived summaries, or code context that agent_b may use as input, and agent_b has shell/write authority to act on that input. Because there is no documented verification step between them, mistaken or manipulated content from agent_a can cascade into incorrect file changes or container operations by agent_b.
conditions: IF agent_b treats agent_a output as authoritative without cross-checking
IF agent_a summarizes files or screenshots that contain errors
IF agent_b uses those summaries to edit or prune container artifacts
mitigations: Require a human check before agent_b acts on agent_a output
Ask agent_b to verify claims against source files
Keep agent_a outputs read-only until reviewed
Use a checklist for any destructive shell action

E_compliance.rationale: Agent_a handles uploaded files, screenshots, voice, and connected IDE code under vendor-mediated processing, while agent_b handles registry credentials, private keys, and vulnerability data in a temporary container. The profiles show different data classes and retention surfaces, so compliance mismatch is plausible even though no specific residency regime is documented.
conditions: IF regulated data such as private keys or vulnerability reports is routed through both agents
IF the operator expects identical retention or residency handling across vendors
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of agent_a unless necessary
Do not pass private keys into agent_b
Document which agent handles which data class
Review vendor retention settings before use
